questions: Where did last year's new client projects actually come from, and how many began with an in-person meeting, a referral from someone who saw the team's work in person, or a local network the office supports, rather than from a digital channel?
Is the 25% cost saving the net figure once you add remote-work stipends, coworking or meeting-room hire for client visits, and any lease exit or reinstatement costs, or is it the gross rent figure?
If you go remote and it harms new-business pace, how hard would it be to get an equivalent office again in a year, and what would the cost and delay be compared with the cost of renewing now?
Can the landlord offer a shorter term, a break clause, a smaller floor area, or a sublet right, so that you can test a hybrid arrangement without committing either way?

The survey asked for more remote days. Did it ask about going fully remote with no office at all, and did the people who want to keep an office, such as juniors, those with poor home setups, or those who are new, answer differently?
How do your newest and most junior designers learn the craft, take critique, and absorb studio standards today, and what would replace that if nobody shared a room?

Which of your biggest clients are comfortable with video check-ins, and do any of them value visiting your studio during a pitch, a workshop, or a presentation of concepts? How do they feel about an agency with no physical base?
Which parts of creative work, such as early concepting, workshops, and last-minute reviews, currently happen better in the room, and what is the evidence that remote tools handle them as well?

What does the team do at home on the two remote days versus the three office days, and have you measured the quality, turnaround, or rework rates on each, or is the sense that remote works based on impressions?
What would make you lose people or fail to hire them if you went remote, such as designers in other time zones or people who valued the office, and how would that affect delivery capacity?
